label: sec:introduction-overview
html:
The starting point is a collection of observations about how an observer interacts with the world. Colours are seen, and three of them mix to produce white. An observer moves around, rotates, and looks from different angles, yet the things measured do not depend on where the observer stands or which way it faces. Time flows in one direction, and observers are carried along with it. Three-fold structure recurs throughout nature — three colours, three generations of matter, three-fold chirality — too insistently to be coincidence; it asks for explanation rather than stipulation. Multiple observers share the same world; they do not each illuminate a private universe but navigate a common landscape.

Some observations run deeper. Observers measure, record, and compare, and the comparisons are consistent: there is a pairing between what is observed and the instruments used. Smooth change is the rule across scales, so linear approximation describes the world from planetary orbits to particle scattering, with integration and differentiation as its native operations. Things occupy space, and that space can be measured — the universe has volume. There is the experience of choice: an observer decides what to measure and when, and the decision shapes what is recorded. Whether that experience reflects something in the structure of the world, or only ignorance of it, is a question rather than a premise; the paper returns to it when observation is treated as a process inside the structure (Measurement and Observation). Even the capacity for computation — to reason, count, and calculate — seems woven into the fabric rather than added on.

One assumption is deliberately left out: that the constants of nature are constant. A physical theory usually takes its constants as fixed numbers, measured once and then held still. If they are allowed to vary — not arbitrarily, but in a controlled, algebraic way — how does that change the mechanics, or more precisely the mechanics of observation? That is the question the paper asks, and the substrate parameter below is the form it takes.

Einstein taught that geometry and mass are bound together: spacetime is not a passive stage on which matter performs, but a participant shaped by the matter it contains. The motivating hope here is that a similar bond holds one level down, between the algebra of processes and the mass and interactions of what those processes describe. The algebraic counterpart of curvature is torsion — the failure of two operations to commute — and the paper asks how much of the structure of particles that failure can carry. Gravity itself is taken up in its own chapter (Gravity and Spacetime Emergence).

Heisenberg wrote that "what we observe is not nature in itself but nature exposed to our method of questioning" [heisenberg1958]. So the question is not what the universe is but what its mechanics do — how its processes compose and transform. Wigner found the effectiveness of mathematics in describing nature "unreasonable", a "wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve" [wigner1960]. The approach of this paper is to take that unreasonableness not as a mystery to be explained but as a principle to be axiomatised: the paper posits that the observable universe is the mathematical structure its own observations force, so that the fit between mathematics and the world is built in rather than discovered.

The natural home for such a structure is category theory, the study of how processes combine. A category records objects and the processes (morphisms) between them, and says how processes compose; a monoidal category also says how two processes run side by side. The language describes structure and transformation without committing to any picture of what the underlying objects "really are". The guiding example is familiar from a first course on Lie groups: the finite-dimensional representations of \mathrm{SU}(2), with their tensor products, duals, and the forgetful map that remembers only the underlying vector space. From that data alone the Tannaka–Krein theorem reconstructs the group itself (Tannaka–Krein reconstruction); the symmetry is recovered from how its representations compose rather than assumed in advance.

The central thesis is that the everyday observations above, once stated carefully, single out one kind of structure: a category of processes rich enough to integrate, to differentiate, and to be measured against. Each observation becomes one ingredient. Duality — every process has a reverse — is the rigidity of the category. Consistent measurement is a fibre functor \tau, which sends each object to the vector space an instrument reads. Integration is a trace: on the \mathrm{SU}(2) example it is exactly the Haar integral over the group (Frobenius pairing on \mathrm{SU}(2)). Volume is the requirement that this trace be non-degenerate. A structure that meets all of these requirements, including that its states be observable and its measurements consistent, is called a quantum observable universe (QOU) (definition). The force of the thesis is that the observations determine the ingredients; nothing else is added by hand.

This starting point is relational in the sense Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz set out in his 1715--1716 correspondence with Samuel Clarke [leibniz-clarke1717, earman1989]: sequential composition (\circ) records the chronological order of successions, the monoidal product and braiding (\otimes, \sigma) record the order of coexistences, and the Principle of the Identity of Indiscernibles equates processes that agree on every closed trace pairing. On the n-strand Iwahori--Hecke braid algebra H_n(q) equipped with the Jones--Markov trace \tau_q at parameter z = q^3/(q^2 + 1), the trace radical \mathrm{rad}\,\tau_q = \{a \in H_n(q) : \tau_q(a b) = 0 \text{ for all } b\} vanishes for n \le 2 and is nonzero for every n \ge 3, where three-strand antisymmetrisation annihilates all trace pairings and blocks any finite spectral distance on H_n(q) (Gram degeneracy). Quotienting by that null ideal in the algebraic sense of Israel M. Gelfand, Mark A. Naimark, and Irving E. Segal [gelfand-naimark1943, segal1947] yields, for nonzero q \in \mathbb{C} with q^k \neq 1 (k \ge 1), the planar Temperley--Lieb algebra H_n(q)/\mathrm{rad}\,\tau_q \cong TL_n(q + q^{-1}) (Temperley--Lieb trace-radical quotient), on whose faithful state space Marc A. Rieffel's compact quantum metric seminorms [rieffel1999] induce a finite Kantorovich--Rubinstein transport metric (Rieffel quotient faithfulness). Unlike the classical relational mechanics of Julian B. Barbour and Bruno Bertotti [barbour-bertotti1982], which quotients a pre-existing Euclidean configuration space \mathbb{R}^{3N} by rigid motions, and unlike Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics [rovelli1996], which indexes Hilbert-space state vectors to pairs of observers while leaving the spacetime metric external, a quantum observable universe posits no spatial manifold at the outset and enforces inter-observer consistency through the shared fibre functor \tau. Downstream, this relational chain yields strictly pseudoconvex contact Cauchy--Riemann three-manifolds whose canonical circle bundle carries Charles L. Fefferman's kinematic (3, 1) Lorentzian metric, while dynamical Einstein field equations on that four-manifold remain conjectural (Lorentzian circle-bundle lift, Gravity and Spacetime Emergence).

The categorical language then recovers, as internal pieces of the structure, the concepts that describe a universe's mechanics. The Lagrangian is a trace and the action is an integral (categorical action); curvature, the gauge field, and the matter current are specific processes in the category; the Dirac operator is a connection twisted by the system's own internal time-flow (categorical Dirac operator). Each is a construction the axioms allow, not an entry borrowed from the classical dictionary.

Noether taught that every continuous symmetry of a physical system yields a conserved quantity: invariance under rotation gives angular momentum, under translation in time gives energy, under a change of gauge gives charge. Her theorem is the bridge from the symmetries that are observed to the quantities that are measured, and it suggests why a trace should be the notion of integration here: a trace is a device for extracting one number from a symmetric process. Once the structure is deformed by the parameter of the next section, the bridge bends rather than breaks: the conserved quantities acquire corrections, and some identities that held exactly become approximate ones (Noether's theorem in the q-deformed setting).
